# Recall



* All languages have words\, but what is a word?
* We introduced  __pragmatics __ and _ _  __sociolinguistics__
* Words get their meaning from
  * History
  * Morphological processes
  * Usage
* Context matters\!
  * Grammatical AND communicative competence
  * Slang is legit\!

---


![](images/9-Why%20are%20some%20words%20bad%20words_0.jpg)

# But what about “bad words”?



* Slang may be legit\, but what about those words people call “bad”?
  * Curse words\, cuss words\, swear words\, taboo words\, potty words\, expletives\, profanity
  * Which words are “bad”\, and are they legit?
* __Swearing __ \(or cursing\, cussing\, etc\.\) is the use of words that are deemed taboo \(by a community\) to express the emotional state of the speaker
  * Focus =  __connotative__  meaning \(what it implies\)
  * And =  __perception__  \(what it means to hearers\)
* Today we will return to __ historical linguistics\,__   __morphology__ \, and  __pragmatics__

---


![](images/9-Why%20are%20some%20words%20bad%20words_1.png)

# Twitter’s “bad words”


---




* Like all words: history\, morphological processes\, and usage\!
* Let’s start with history\!
* What word do you think this is?
  * Old English  _scitan_ \, from Proto\-Germanic  _\*skit\-_  \(source also of North Frisian  _skitj_ \, Dutch  _schijten_ \, German  _scheissen_ \)\, from Proto\-Indo\-European root  _\*_  _skei_  _\-_  “to cut\, split”\, extension of root  _\*_  _sek_  “to cut”
  * The idea is about separation from the body
  * And it’s related to  _science_ \,  _omniscient_ \, _ _ and  _conscience_ \!


# How do we make “bad words”?

# Media

[https://www\.etymonline\.com/search?q=shit](https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=shit)


---




* __Comparative reconstruction __ is a method used in historical linguistics to uncover vocabulary and structures of an ancestor language by drawing inferences from the evidence remaining in several daughter languages
  * Often dealing with the  _sounds_  of a language
  * You can use the IPA chart in Canvas if you want to know more now \(we’ll do more phonetics soon\)
* So\, with the previous example:
  * _\*_  _skei_  _\- > \*skit\- _ = vowel change\, addition of \[t\] \(though see  _\*_  _sek_  _\-_ \)
  * _\*skit\- > _  _scitan_  _ _ = maybe not a change for k > c \(?\)\, addition of verbal suffix
  * _scitan_  _ _ >  _shit_  = \[sk\] > \[ʃ\]\, loss of inflexion

# There’s a rule!!



* Take a multi\-syllable word
* Break it at the point just before the stress
  * ab\-so\- _lute_ \-ly
* Insert “bad word” before that stress
  * ab\-so\- __freaking__ \-lute\-ly
* Don’t put it anywhere else\!
  * ab\-freaking\-so\-lute\-ly?
  * ab\-so\-lute\-freaking\-ly?

# Why do we use “bad words”?

![](images/9-Why%20are%20some%20words%20bad%20words_5.png)



* It’s usually about emotion\!
  * Neurological\, psychological\, and sociocultural
  * A learned behavior
* Some people talk about it with respect to politeness
  * That’s where pragmatics comes back\!
  * You should know\, however\, that swearing is not universally rude
  * It can be funny\, cathartic\, automatic\, related to brain injury\, etc\.

---


# Doing stuff with language



* Language is the principal means we have to “do stuff”
  * To greet\, compliment\, and insult one another\,
  * To plead or flirt\,
  * To seek and supply information\, and
  * To accomplish hundreds of other daily tasks
* Actions that are carried out through language are called  __speech acts__
  * Such as lying\, promising\, greeting\, etc\.
  * Let’s focus on  __indirect speech acts__


![](images/9-Why%20are%20some%20words%20bad%20words_6.png)

# Politeness


---


![](images/9-Why%20are%20some%20words%20bad%20words_7.png)



* It’s all about “saving face”
* Brown and Levinson \(1987\) discussed the most influential and comprehensive model for understanding politeness –  __face\-saving model__
  * Face = one’s public self\-image
    * Universal notion in human societies
    * Two kinds of face:
      * __Positive face: __ one’s desire to be liked \(See positive politeness…\)
      * __Negative face: __ one’s desire to be left alone \(See negative politeness…\)

---


# Why do we do that?

![](images/9-Why%20are%20some%20words%20bad%20words_8.png)

Think about who you feel comfortable swearing around

Remember that it’s a learned behavior

If swearing is seen as rude by the hearer\, the speaker has violated the hearer’s negative face \(to be left alone\)

Self\-censorship \(to save others’ faces\) potentially threatens the speaker’s positive face \(perhaps swearing is their most charming feature\)

And even if broad social norms make swearing more acceptable in some contexts\, because of their connection to rudeness\, etc\.\, some listeners may find it unwelcome
